h1:
Getting Around Yasothon
How to Arrive and Explore the Province
intro: Yasothon is a small province in the middle of Isaan with no airport and no train line running through it, so most people arrive either by direct intercity bus from Bangkok or by flying into Ubon Ratchathani and driving the last 100 km or so. Once you're here, the standout sights — Phu Tham Phra out in Loeng Nok Tha, and the old riverside town of Maha Chana Chai — sit in opposite directions and are a fair way from the city. We've put the arrival options, rough prices, and in-province distances all in one place so you can plan before you actually set off.

blocks.html: Before planning, it helps to know the lay of the land: Yasothon has neither an airport nor a train station within the province. The northeastern rail line runs through Khon Kaen and Ubon but skips Yasothon entirely, and the nearest airport is Ubon Ratchathani, about 100 km away. That leaves two main approaches — take a direct bus from Bangkok straight into the city, or fly into Ubon (some people choose Roi Et or Khon Kaen instead) and drive in — then sort out how to get around the province once you've arrived.

The bus is the option most people use, because it runs straight into the city and the fare is easy on the wallet. Buses leave from Mo Chit 2 Bus Terminal (Chatuchak) in Bangkok and arrive at the Yasothon Bus Terminal, which sits right in town, so getting on to your hotel is straightforward. The Bangkok–Yasothon distance is roughly 530–570 km and the trip takes about 8–9 hours depending on stops and traffic.

items: Main operators — Nakhonchai Air, Cherdchai Tour and a few others run this route several times a day. Some services continue past Yasothon on to Amnat Charoen or Mukdahan.
Rough fares — air-conditioned/first-class seats start around ฿440–520, while 32-seat VIP coaches run about ฿520–570 depending on the class and operator.

Departure times — there are both morning and overnight services. The late runs (roughly 19:30–22:00) get you in by early morning, so you sleep on board and wake up there — a popular choice. Morning departures around 08:30 are there too if you'd rather watch the scenery go by.

Booking — you can book ahead online through busticket.in.th, Nakhonchai Air, busonlineticket or 12go, or just buy at the counter at Mo Chit 2. During festivals — especially the Bun Bang Fai rocket festival in May — book early, as seats fill up fast.

blocks.title: Picking the right bus departure
blocks.html: If you want to save a day of your trip, take an overnight sleeper: it leaves in the evening and reaches Yasothon around dawn to early morning, so you get a full day of sightseeing without losing one to travel. But if you get carsick easily, or you'd like to see the Isaan rice fields along the way, a morning departure is the more comfortable call.

blocks.text: Fly into Ubon Ratchathani, then drive to Yasothon

blocks.html: Since Yasothon has no airport, people who'd rather fly usually land at Ubon Ratchathani Airport (UBP), which has frequent flights from Don Muang and Suvarnabhumi at fares that are usually reasonable, then drive the remaining 98–103 km into Yasothon — about 1.5 to 2 hours. This works well if you don't fancy a long overnight bus ride.

items: Airlines to Ubon — Thai AirAsia, Thai Lion Air, Nok Air, Thai Vietjet and Thai Smile all fly in and out of Ubon several times a day, with advance fares often starting around ฿900–1,500 one way.
Vans/buses Ubon–Yasothon — these run throughout the day from Ubon's bus terminal, with fares around ฿100–150 and a journey of about 1.5 hours. Good if you're on a budget.

Direct vans from Ubon Airport to Yasothon — there are private van/shuttle services running from the airport straight to Yasothon, costing around ฿350 per person (or charter the whole vehicle by arrangement). Handy if there are a few of you.

Why Ubon over the alternatives — lots of flights, flexible schedules, and you can fold a bit of Ubon into the same trip. Some people fly into Roi Et or Khon Kaen instead, but Ubon has the most frequent flights.

blocks.title: Worth knowing before you fly into Ubon
blocks.html: If you're flying into Ubon and transferring by road, check what time the last Ubon–Yasothon van/bus runs, because the final service usually isn't very late. If your flight lands in the evening, you may need to overnight in Ubon or charter a shuttle — plan for it ahead of time so you're not stranded at the airport.

blocks.text: Renting a car — the best value for Yasothon

blocks.html: Several of Yasothon's best sights are outside the city and aren't well served by public transport — Phu Tham Phra in Loeng Nok Tha in particular sits a full 85 km out. So renting and driving yourself is the option that makes the most sense if you want to hit Loeng Nok Tha, Maha Chana Chai and Kut Chum in one trip. In Yasothon town there are local rental shops plus options you can book through platforms, but if you're coming via Ubon it's more convenient to rent at Ubon Airport from the start and drive in, since the airport has plenty of big-name rental desks to choose from.

items: Rental prices — a small sedan starts around ฿700–900 per day, while a 7-seat SUV/pickup runs about ฿1,200–1,800 per day, usually including first-class insurance and a full tank at pickup.

Where to rent — there are a handful of local shops in Yasothon town, but fewer choices than in bigger cities. Booking through Drivehub or a major brand is easier if you pick the car up at Ubon Airport and drive into Yasothon.
Documents — you'll need a driving licence and an ID card/passport. Some operators don't take a deposit. Always photograph the car all the way around before you take it.

Driving in the province — Yasothon town is small, traffic is light and parking is easy. The roads out to the other districts are good-quality highways (Route 23 into town, Route 212 up to Loeng Nok Tha) and pleasant to drive, but petrol stations are spread out once you're out of town, so top up before any long stretch.

blocks.text: Getting around town without a car

blocks.html: If you're only seeing the town itself — places like the Ban Singha Tha quarter, Wat Maha That, Phra That Kong Khao Noi (just outside town) and Phaya Thaen Park — you don't really need to rent a car, because the in-town sights are close together and you can walk or hop on a songthaew or motorbike taxi. But if you're heading out to far districts like Loeng Nok Tha or Maha Chana Chai, public transport gets awkward.

items: Songthaew — these run around town and out to nearby districts, with in-town fares in the low tens of baht. Always ask the price before you get on.
Motorbike taxis — found at junctions and outside markets, good for short hops around town.

Motorbike rental — shops rent them out for around ฿200–300 a day, ideal for a solo traveler or a couple not going too far. But for the run up to Loeng Nok Tha, a car is the better call given the distance.
Ride-hailing apps — coverage in Yasothon town isn't as dense as in big cities, and at quiet times you may wait a while, so build in some buffer.

blocks.text: In-province distances to the main sights

blocks.html: Here are the approximate distances from Yasothon town to the spots people ask about most, measured from the city center and rounded off so you can gauge travel time. As you'll see, Phu Tham Phra in Loeng Nok Tha is the furthest out, while Maha Chana Chai is off in the other direction — so plan your route well to avoid doubling back.

items.name: Ban Singha Tha quarter (city center)
items.blurb: The old-town quarter of vintage Chinese-Western shophouses right in the center — a landmark you can walk to from many in-town hotels.
items.meta: In town · a few minutes' walk or drive

items.name: Phra That Kong Khao Noi (Yasothon town)
items.blurb: An old rice-basket-shaped stupa, a legend bound up with Yasothon, sitting on the eastern edge of town — a short drive away.

items.name: Phaya Thaen Park
items.blurb: A riverside park on the Lam Thuan in the center, with the Phaya Thaen rocket plaza and rest areas — good for a walk or a cycle, close to town.
items.meta: In town · a few minutes' drive

items.name: Maha Chana Chai district
items.blurb: An old town on the Chi River, known for pla som (fermented fish) and old temples, off to the south of the province on a good-quality highway.

items.name: Kut Chum district
items.blurb: A district known for organic rice and indigo-dyed cloth, with waterfalls and nature, off to the north — often a stop on the way up to Loeng Nok Tha.

items.name: Loeng Nok Tha district
items.blurb: The province's northernmost district, the gateway to Phu Tham Phra and the nature along the Mukdahan border — a long drive north up Route 212.

items.name: Phu Tham Phra (Loeng Nok Tha)
items.blurb: A small hill with a cave enshrining many ancient Buddha images, set in shady forest with a waterfall in the rainy season — about 12 km past Loeng Nok Tha town along Route 212, then a turn up the hill.

items.name: Ubon Ratchathani Airport (arrival/departure transfer)
items.blurb: The nearest airport, used to fly in and out and then transfer into Yasothon, or to fold a bit of Ubon into the same trip.

blocks.title: Plan your route to save fuel
blocks.html: Kut Chum and Loeng Nok Tha–Phu Tham Phra lie north along the same road, so you can do them on a single day: head out early, stop at Kut Chum first, then carry on up to Loeng Nok Tha and Phu Tham Phra. Maha Chana Chai is off to the south in the other direction, so it's better saved for a separate day — that saves both time and fuel compared with driving back and forth.

blocks.text: So which option should you pick?

items.name: Cheapest
items.blurb: The overnight Mo Chit–Yasothon bus: wake up just as you reach the city, a fare in the low hundreds, dropping you right in town.

items.name: Fastest
items.blurb: Fly into Ubon and rent a car at the airport on the spot, then drive into Yasothon in about 1.5–2 hours — the biggest time-saver.

items.name: Easiest to get around
items.blurb: Arrive however you like, but rent a car to drive yourself around the province — that's how you cover Loeng Nok Tha, Phu Tham Phra and Maha Chana Chai in full.

faq.q: How long does the bus from Bangkok to Yasothon take?
faq.a: The Bangkok–Yasothon distance is roughly 530–570 km, and the bus takes about 8–9 hours depending on stops and the time of day. Buses leave from Mo Chit 2 and arrive at the Yasothon Bus Terminal in town, with fares starting around ฿440 up to ฿570 depending on the class. The main operators are Nakhonchai Air and Cherdchai Tour.

faq.q: Does Yasothon have an airport? If I want to fly, where do I land?
faq.a: Yasothon has no airport and no train line running through it. If you want to fly, the nearest airport is Ubon Ratchathani, about 98–103 km away, from where you take a van/bus or rent a car into Yasothon — roughly 1.5–2 hours. Some people fly into Roi Et or Khon Kaen instead, but Ubon has the most frequent flights.

faq.q: How do I get from Ubon Airport to Yasothon, and how much does it cost?
faq.a: From Ubon Airport there are several ways into Yasothon. Vans/buses from Ubon's bus terminal cost around ฿100–150, while private vans/shuttles running straight from the airport to Yasothon are about ฿350 per person. Or you can rent a car at Ubon Airport and drive in yourself, which is convenient and takes around 1.5–2 hours.

faq.q: How much does car rental in Yasothon cost, and where should I rent?
faq.a: A small sedan starts around ฿700–900 per day, and a 7-seat SUV or pickup runs about ฿1,200–1,800 per day, usually including first-class insurance and a full tank at pickup. Yasothon town has a handful of local shops but limited choice, so if you're coming via Ubon it's best to rent at Ubon Airport from the start, where the bigger desks give you more options.

faq.q: Is it far from town to Phu Tham Phra in Loeng Nok Tha and to Maha Chana Chai?
faq.a: Phu Tham Phra is in Loeng Nok Tha district, Kut Hae sub-district, about 85 km from Yasothon town — roughly a 1.5-hour drive along Route 212, past Loeng Nok Tha town (about 69 km from the city) and then a further 12 km or so. Maha Chana Chai district is to the south, about 41 km away, around a 45-minute drive. The two are in opposite directions, so it's best to visit them on separate days.
